question:
Patient note:
A 64-year-old woman is evaluated this morning in the short-stay pre-operative bay before transfer to the procedure room for a planned bedside irrigation, nail-bed repair, and simple layered closure of a 1.4-cm laceration on the volar surface of the left index finger that occurred while she was maneuvering crutches; the hand service estimates no more than fifteen minutes of tourniquet time under digital block, and she is expected to return to her inpatient room immediately afterward. She has been confined to her hospital bed for the past nine days on strict limb-elevation orders after sustaining a closed, non-displaced inter-trochanteric fracture of the right femur when she tripped on a loose rug at home three weeks ago. Orthopedics elected non-operative management because of the favorable alignment, and on admission day a bulky, above-knee fiberglass immobilizer was applied from groin to ankle; daily progress notes document only brief transfers with a seated pivot onto a bedside commode and otherwise uninterrupted bed rest. As a result, nursing records show fewer than 200 cumulative steps since arrival, and physical therapy sessions have been limited to isometric quadriceps contractions and ankle pumps performed in the supine position. The encasing cast remains intact this morning with clean edges, no foul odor, and capillary refill brisk in all toes; sensations to light touch and pinprick over the plantar and dorsal aspects of the foot are preserved, and posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable 2+. She reports mild aching around the hip that is well controlled by scheduled acetaminophen and intermittent oral hydromorphone; no breakthrough doses have been needed overnight. Prior to the fall she lived independently, performed household chores, and walked two miles daily for exercise despite longstanding superficial venous dilatations over both calves that she first noticed in her late thirties; inspection today reveals tortuous blue vessels tracking along the medial saphenous distribution, but there is no pitting edema, calf tenderness, or side-to-side circumference discrepancy. She has never experienced unilateral leg swelling, crampy calf pain, pleuritic chest discomfort, or imaging-confirmed thromboembolic disease, and none of her relatives have required anticoagulation for idiopathic clot. Her medical history otherwise includes diet-controlled type 2 diabetes and well-treated primary hypertension; she denies chronic lung disease, episodes of pump failure, inflammatory bowel symptoms, malignancy, prior myocardial infarction, or cerebrovascular events. The current admission is her first hospitalization in more than a decade, and she underwent no operations or endoscopic procedures during the preceding month before the fracture. She has not worn a splint, brace, or walking boot on any other limb, and no peripherally inserted or tunneled central catheters have ever been placed; present venous access consists only of a single 22-gauge peripheral cannula in the left forearm running 0.9 % saline at 50 mL/hr. Daily oral medications include lisinopril 20 mg, metformin 500 mg twice, and a multivitamin; she takes no estrogen preparations, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet drugs. She quit smoking twelve years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, consumes half a glass of wine on holidays, and denies recreational substance use. Early-morning vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, heart rate 84 beats/min regular, blood pressure 134/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air; body mass index is 26 kg/m². She is alert and conversant, oriented to date and location, and airway evaluation shows Mallampati class II with intact dentition and full cervical range. Sclerae are anicteric, neck veins are flat with the head elevated 30°, cardiac examination reveals a regular rhythm with normal S₁ and S₂ and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with good diaphragmatic excursion during incentive-spirometer coaching. Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and without organomegaly; bowel sounds are present. The right lower limb casted from groin to ankle rests on two pillows, the heel is floated, and there is no skin breakdown over the sacrum or greater trochanter. The contralateral extremity is warm, well perfused, and free of edema or cords, and bilateral calf circumferences measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosities are 35 cm with less than 0.5 cm difference. Neurologic screening shows 5/5 strength in upper extremities except for pain-limited flexion at the injured finger, intact sensation throughout, and symmetric reflexes. Laboratory studies drawn at 05:30 through the peripheral line demonstrate hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, leukocytes 7.2 ×10⁹/L, platelets 248 ×10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, creatinine 0.88 mg/dL, AST 21 U/L, ALT 19 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained on admission displays clear lung fields and normal cardiac silhouette, and a baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram yesterday showed normal sinus rhythm at 78 beats/min without ST-T abnormalities. Sequential pneumatic compression sleeves were applied to both calves on hospital day 1 but remain off for transport; no pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis has yet been administered because the orthopedic and anesthesia teams prefer to reassess hematologic risk once the finger repair is complete. She has been nil per os since midnight, last voided at 0600, and verbal consent for the procedure, including potential need for a superficial skin graft should primary closure prove inadequate, was reaffirmed at bedside fifteen minutes ago.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE risk score sums weighted perioperative risk factors. The BMI threshold matters in this case:
- Hip fracture within the past month: intertrochanteric fracture three weeks ago → 5.
- Age 61–74 years: age 64 → 2.
- Bed confinement >72 hours: nine days with only brief commode transfers → 2.
- Immobilizing leg cast within the past month: current groin-to-ankle cast → 2.
- Visible varicose veins → 1.
- Planned minor surgery: brief finger repair under digital block → 1.
These factors sum to 5 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 13. This is the total if no BMI point is assigned. The standard Caprini criterion of BMI >25 kg/m² would add 1 for her BMI of 26, giving 14 rather than 13.
Final answer: 13
